source_text: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, oh daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them.
modern_text: Tell me, Muse, of that clever hero who wandered far and wide after he destroyed the famous city of Troy. He visited many cities and learned the customs of many peoples. He suffered greatly at sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men home safely. But no matter what he did, he could not save his companions—they died through their own reckless folly when they ate the cattle of the sun god Helios. So the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me about all these things, daughter of Zeus, from whatever source you know them.

source_text: “‘You will find the other rock lie lower, but they are so close together that there is not more than a bow-shot between them. [A large fig tree in full leaf grows upon it], and under it lies the sucking whirlpool of Charybdis. Three times in the day does she vomit forth her waters, and three times she sucks them down again; see that you be not there when she is sucking, for if you are, Neptune himself could not save you; you must hug the Scylla side and drive ship by as fast as you can, for you had better lose six men than your whole crew.’
modern_text: "The other rock lies lower, but they're so close together there's barely a bowshot between them. A large fig tree grows on it in full leaf, and beneath it lies Charybdis' sucking whirlpool. Three times each day she spits up the waters, and three times she sucks them down again. Make sure you're not there when she's sucking them down, for if you are, not even Poseidon could save you. You must hug Scylla's side and drive your ship past as fast as possible, because it's better to lose six men than your entire crew."

source_text: Ulysses answered, “Madam, I have foresworn rugs and blankets from the day that I left the snowy ranges of Crete to go on shipboard. I will lie as I have lain on many a sleepless night hitherto. Night after night have I passed in any rough sleeping place, and waited for morning. Nor, again, do I like having my feet washed; I shall not let any of the young hussies about your house touch my feet; but, if you have any old and respectable woman who has gone through as much trouble as I have, I will allow her to wash them.”
modern_text: Odysseus answered, "Madam, I have foresworn rugs and blankets from the day that I left the snowy ranges of Crete to go on shipboard. I will lie as I have lain on many a sleepless night hitherto. Night after night have I passed in any rough sleeping place, and waited for morning. Nor, again, do I like having my feet washed; I shall not let any of the young hussies about your house touch my feet; but, if you have any old and respectable woman who has gone through as much trouble as I have, I will allow her to wash them."

source_text: Ulysses slept in the cloister upon an undressed bullock’s hide, on the top of which he threw several skins of the sheep the suitors had eaten, and Eurynome threw a cloak over him after he had laid himself down. There, then, Ulysses lay wakefully brooding upon the way in which he should kill the suitors; and by and by, the women who had been in the habit of misconducting themselves with them, left the house giggling and laughing with one another. This made Ulysses very angry, and he doubted whether to get up and kill every single one of them then and there, or to let them sleep one more and last time with the suitors. His heart growled within him, and as a bitch with puppies growls and shows her teeth when she sees a stranger, so did his heart growl with anger at the evil deeds that were being done: but he beat his breast and said, “Heart, be still, you had worse than this to bear on the day when the terrible Cyclops ate your brave companions; yet you bore it in silence till your cunning got you safe out of the cave, though you made sure of being killed.”
modern_text: Odysseus slept in the courtyard on a raw bull's hide, with several sheepskins thrown over it from the animals the suitors had devoured. Eurynome covered him with a cloak after he lay down. There Odysseus lay sleepless, brooding over how he would kill the suitors. Soon the servant women who had been sleeping with the suitors came giggling and laughing out of the house together. This made Odysseus furious, and he wondered whether to leap up and kill every one of them on the spot, or let them enjoy one final night with the suitors. His heart growled within him like a mother dog protecting her puppies, baring her teeth at a stranger. But he struck his chest and said, "Heart, be still. You endured worse than this when the terrible Cyclops devoured your brave companions. Yet you bore it in silence until your cunning got you safely out of that cave, though you thought you were doomed."
